questions.q: A narrator insists he was a loyal, contented servant, but the novel keeps showing us what he gave up. What is Booth's term for him?
questions.explain: His account conflicts with the norms of the work, so the reader sees past him.

questions.q: What does Booth mean by the implied author?
choices: The ghostwriter behind a celebrity memoir
The narrator of a first-person novel
The sensibility a reader infers from all the work's choices
questions.explain: It's distinct from both the flesh-and-blood author and the narrator.

questions.q: A workshop leader says, "Never tell, always show." How would Booth respond?
choices: Telling is a legitimate tool, and showing is also a set of authorial choices
He'd agree: commentary always weakens fiction
Telling is fine only in the climax
questions.explain: Booth argued against the rule; the question is the effect on the reader.

questions.q: What makes a novel polyphonic in Bakhtin's sense?
choices: It's narrated by several people in turn
Its characters are independent voices the author doesn't overrule
It uses free indirect style throughout
questions.explain: Polyphony is about unmerged, fully valid consciousnesses, not just multiple narrators.

questions.q: "Ted watched the orchestra through stupid tears." Why is this free indirect style?
choices: The word 'stupid' is Ted's judgment, absorbed into third-person narration
questions.explain: Narration takes on the character's own words without quotation marks.

questions.q: Which stage device most directly gives one character control of the audience's point of view?
choices: Direct address, as in Richard III's asides or Tom's narration in The Glass Menagerie
questions.explain: Direct address and onstage narrators make one character our guide, reliable or not.

questions.q: Bakhtin claimed drama is alien to genuine polyphony. What's a common reply from theatre scholars?
choices: A stage of embodied, contending voices is dialogic by nature
Plays have no point of view at all
questions.explain: Many argue drama's competing live voices make it inherently dialogic.

questions.q: A reporter writes a feature entirely from inside a subject's head. What does the point-of-view choice demand?
choices: Reporting that justifies knowing those thoughts
questions.explain: Interior access in journalism has to be earned by interviews and evidence.

ideas: Every novel implies an author, a sensibility behind its choices, against whom we measure the narrator.
Telling is as legitimate a fictional tool as showing; even the most dramatic scene is a rhetorical choice.
The greatest novels let characters' voices stand as independent, unmerged consciousnesses rather than subordinating them to the author's.
Every word we use already carries other people's intentions, so all speech is a reply in an ongoing dialogue.
